#7508. Publishers: Agentic AI Isn’t About Pricing, But Whether You Get Any Bids At All

The agentic skeptics have the better argument right now.

Anthony Katsur, who runs IAB Tech Lab, expects “several false starts” and years of experimentation and alignment across platforms, agencies and publishers. Razorfish called the mood around agentic AI inevitable – but incremental – at CES back in January.

And Digiday’s research in January found that 54% of 142 brand and agency professionals say their companies don’t use agentic AI in their workflows at all. That is the buy side reporting on itself.

Anyone telling publishers they are already behind on agentic AI is selling something.

However, there’s a fundamental difference between agentic AI and the “inevitable” industry shifts that came before it. Each of those shifts required somebody to build and pay for new integration, and the parties who had to pay disagreed about what to build. The variable is sunk integration cost.

Agentic is the first shift where buyers already paid that bill.

Agentic AI doesn’t face the same barriers. Fully autonomous media buying may still be years away, but AI agents don’t need new pipes or industrywide standards to start evaluating inventory, informing bidding decisions and optimizing spend. They can operate through existing programmatic infrastructure, using integrations the buy side has already built and paid for.

On April 8, 2026, Microsoft ended a relationship with Dentsu that ran for more than a decade and moved its global media planning and buying to Publicis. That mandate carried a price tag the trade press puts between $700 million and $1.2 billion. The media appointment sat inside a larger announcement about embedding agentic AI across the marketing workflow: agents on Microsoft Fabric, informed by Epsilon, deciding which segments matter and deploying media against them.

Asked why Publicis keeps winning without pitches, Arthur Sadoun said clients now understand “it’s about identity.” Publicis also agreed in May 2026 to acquire LiveRamp, a deal the FTC cleared in October subject to a 5-year neutrality order. Once it closes, one of the two largest buyers of publisher inventory will own more of the identity layer that its own agents reason over.

Those agents buy media. Media clears in auctions. Publishers get paid in those auctions.

The industry’s experience with bid shading shows how quickly new buying logic can reshape auctions.

Exchanges began moving to first-price auctions in 2017. Google announced Ad Manager’s move to first-price in March 2019 and finished four months later. Bid shading, a strategy for avoiding paying too much in first-price auctions, spread across SSPs and then DSPs within months via existing integrations, without new infrastructure or industrywide standards.

Publishers, meanwhile, were left to understand bid shading’s impact through their clearing-price reports and adjust their pricing floors accordingly.

Call bid shading machine learning rather than agentic if you prefer. But what’s different this time with agentic is what the logic decides. Shading optimized the price of a bid you were already making. But identity-informed agents decide what inventory is worth a bid at all.

The distinction matters. Publishers risk losing opportunities before their inventory even reaches an auction.

Think of agentic logic as being divided into two halves. IAB research underscores the divide between AI-powered decision-making and autonomous execution. Among 360 digital video buyers surveyed this February and March, 96% see a role for agentic AI in programmatic and RTB, and 63% expect that role to be an optimization layer that improves bidding.

But current adoption, in IAB’s own words, is centered on decision support rather than the purchase decision itself. AI-based deal execution and negotiation for video campaigns sits at 28%. Forty percent of buyers require human approval before an agent acts. That is the shape of it: Agents run freely where no money is committed and get gated where it is.

When Katsur predicts those agentic false starts, he is describing the execution half, and he is right about it.

But the decision-making half is already gaining traction. Among video buyers spending $50 million or more a year, 63% are using or planning to use agents for inventory discovery and evaluation, against 30% of smaller buyers. The largest budgets in the market are pointing agents at deciding which inventory is worth considering.

The exposure is not whether agents will pay a premium for your inventory. It is whether your inventory survives evaluation. Fail that, and you will not be outbid in some future auction. You will not be in the running at all.

Which means the work is the same work it has always been, and it pays now. Publishers don’t need to wait for agentic standards to mature to prepare. Much of the necessary groundwork can also improve performance in today’s auctions.

Here are three steps to take, none of which require knowing which standard wins:

These steps can strengthen inventory evaluation and match rates today, regardless of how quickly autonomous buying develops.

Remember: In 2019, the publishers who understood their own floors before the auction changed did fine. The ones who only learned about the change in buy-side decisioning from their revenue reports did not.

With agentic AI, waiting for fully autonomous transactions could mean missing the more consequential shift already underway.

#7504. TIME’s AI Agents Do The Coordinating, And Its Sellers Still Do The Selling

If an AI agent can turn an advertiser’s RFP into a proposal in minutes, what’s left for a publisher’s ad sales team to do?

A lot more selling, said Mark Howard, TIME’s chief operating officer.

In the recent past, when an RFP would come in from a potential buyer, it would kick off a flurry of activity – and a series of labor-intensive tasks – that had little to do with actual selling. Once a rep logged the RFP details in Salesforce, the hand-offs would begin.

Alerts would fire off via Slack, product experts would be dragged into Google Meets to map out inventory across a large product suite and notes would get blasted over email. Meanwhile, the sales team would spend days manually coordinating across various platforms to stitch together a response.

“Premium media sales is still a highly personal, relationship-driven business,” Howard said, “and sellers lose too much time playing coordinator.”

To help ease that operational bottleneck, TIME has been working with Kana, a startup founded by Tom Chavez and Vivek Vaidya, serial ad tech entrepreneurs and the dudes who co-founded Krux, the DMP Salesforce bought roughly a decade ago.

In 2019, the pair launched super{set}, a nontraditional VC firm that co-founds, builds and incubates data and AI startups.

Kana, which came out of stealth in February with a $15 million seed funding round, builds AI agents that take over the grunt work of the ad business.

TIME is using two of Kana’s agents. One works alongside the sales team, reading RFPs and drafting proposals. The other works with ad ops, watching live campaigns and recommending what to do when one starts to fall behind.

The sales agent draws on what Vaidya refers to as a “knowledge graph,” a shared pool of context Kana builds by pulling from TIME’s Salesforce CRM, order management system and ad server, both direct and programmatic.

It also brings in data from live campaigns, which is atypical for a pre-sales tool, Vaidya said. Once a deal closes, this type of data is usually the domain of ad ops, which uses it to look back at how a campaign performed, not to plan the next overture.

The sales agent can proactively turn that information into raw material for pitches.

“We do the research, we look at historical data and we look at similar advertisers,” Vaidya said. “Then a salesperson can go in and start ideating on new proposals for advertisers that TIME hasn’t even sold to yet.”

But the relationship itself still belongs to the salesperson, Howard said, and TIME isn’t looking to automate that or make it into an agentic process.

“We don’t do it with our journalism,” he said, “and we’re not going to do it with our sales.”

Well, at least, “that isn’t the plan for now,” he added.

Once a deal closes, the work shifts to ad ops, and to Kana’s second agent.

Ad ops teams already have dashboards that show them when a campaign is underdelivering or not pacing properly. What those dashboards don’t say, though, is what to do about it, Vaidya said.

The Kana agent answers that for each campaign and recommends a fix, like changing trafficking, pacing or budget, so a shortfall doesn’t turn into a make-good.

TIME’s revenue operations team, meanwhile, is also using the tool, Howard said, and he’s seen “a significant increase in what they’re able to accomplish in any given day or week.” It’s also helping with budget planning.

“And not just for how we’re going to finish this year and how Q1 looks, but actual 2027 modeling,” Howard said. “It’s a whole new world when you can have these kinds of insights delivered to you.”

Between proposals and pacing, agents now cover most of a deal’s life cycle, so there’s technically nothing stopping a publisher’s agent from dealing directly with an advertiser’s agent while the sales rep heads out for a three-martini lunch.

Kana could build that, Vaidya said. Put an MCP server (a standard way for AI agents to connect to other software) in front of the proposal agent, and it would be able to talk to an advertiser’s agents tomorrow.

“That’s a technology problem, which is easy to solve,” he said.

Selling is still built on relationships, Howard said, and agents doing the deal is “just not in our game plan.”

#7499. Skydance Efforts to Merge Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery Have Only Just Begun

Not surprisingly, Skydance’s first post-merger earnings report was a little bit messy.

Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) closed five weeks ago on October 4, just after the third quarter ended on September 30. So, investors who wanted Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz to pull back the curtain on the combined entity’s finances on Monday will have to wait another quarter for the full picture.

At the same time, Paramount Skydance’s previous merger between Paramount and Skydance closed smack dab in the middle of Q3 last year on August 7, making growth comparisons across the same periods in 2025 and 2026 a bit more annoying to track.

At least it seems that Paramount Skydance did pretty well for itself – excluding WBD, of course. The business earned $7 billion in revenue last quarter at a year-over-year growth rate of 5%, which puts it on track for the high end of its 2026 profitability outlook.

Direct-to-consumer revenue grew almost twice as much at 11% to $2.5 billion, and Paramount+ revenue in particular grew 21% YoY to just over $2.1 billion.

Overall advertising revenue for the quarter came out to $1.89 billion, which was actually a slight 3% decrease compared to the previous quarter of $1.94 billion.

Part of that gap was likely due to an 8% decline in advertising revenue within Paramount Skydance’s TV Media revenue, which also decreased 7% YoY to $3 billion.

The mergers will continue until morale improves

But just because the newly combined Skydance isn’t financially reporting on the WBD side of the business yet, doesn’t mean it’s not fully willing to take credit for the company’s wins.

As the company’s shareholder letter notes, when combined, Paramount and Warner Bros. produced seven of the top 10 most-watched series across linear and streaming. Behind YouTube, Skydance also now represents the second largest media distributor by share of total US TV time according to Nielsen’s Gauge report.

Skydance also announced that it plans to launch a bundle of HBO Max and Paramount+ at the beginning of 2027. Ellison called this “a first step towards a fully unified offering,” something he expressed interest in doing long before the merger closed.

In the meantime, behind-the-scenes consolidation has been doing well on the Paramount side. Take Pluto, which was acquired by Paramount Skydance in August of last year and now represents 75 monthly active users. Paramount+ and Pluto are finally unified on the same tech stack, according to Ellison. He expects the migration of HBO Max onto that same stack to go even faster.

Skydance is also targeting at least $6 billion of “annual run-rate synergies” – meaning, post-merger cost savings – over the next three years.

Much of those savings will come from streamlining Skydance’s marketing costs and its tech stack, said new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz. That streamlining will involve optimizing (which feels like a fancy euphemism for “cutting back on”) its spending with third-party vendors.

On the other side of the dreaded s-word, the company will also be able to drive revenue synergy with both distribution and advertising within its television business. This will allow advertisers to purchase media across the entire portfolio, which will be especially helpful for Skydance’s sports offerings now that CBS Sports and TNT Sports are under one roof, said Kreiz.

Of course, the antitrust settlement that paved the way for Skydance’s merger still requires separate negotiations of Paramount and Warner Bros.’ cable portfolios. But the rest of the company’s TV business – especially its streaming services, of course – is poised for further consolidation.

“Once that’s on one unified tech stack, it really does position ourselves to really be competitive with anyone,” added Ellison.

TIME is using AI agents to draft proposals and troubleshoot campaigns – but not to replace the human relationships that drive ad sales.

Viant also used its earnings call to announce the close of its acquisition of AI video creative production platform Waymark for $20 million in cash, a deal designed to help advertisers make more CTV ads faster.

Despite the news, Viant’s stock was down around 7% in after-hours trading. It’s not immediately clear why, but spending could be a factor. Viant expects its costs to rise about 25% next quarter, partly because of acquisitions like TVision and Waymark that aren’t expected to bring in meaningful revenue yet.

But hey, maybe that’s just the price of going all in on CTV, and Viant isn’t hedging.

Tim Vanderhook, Viant’s CEO, hyped Waymark as the start of an “era of generative ad creative for CTV” and said it could attract thousands if not millions of new advertisers to connected TV.

But where does that leave the open web? In the corner with no Patrick Swayze to save it.

During the Q&A portion of the call, Laura Martin, an analyst at Needham & Company, asked how Viant plans to keep growing revenue when the open internet is starting to shrivel like a slug in salt and even its longstanding champions, like Reddit, are throwing in the towel.

In response, Tim Vanderhook said that the open internet is only “10% or less” of Viant’s business and is “certainly not driving the growth rates we’re seeing now.”

As far as Viant is concerned, every dollar leaving the open web is a dollar headed toward CTV.

Advertisers are shifting more of their budgets away from display and online video towards more addressable and “premium” environments, Vanderhook said, which he believes will “end up being a catalyst for us next year.”

Still, just because budgets are moving to CTV, doesn’t mean every advertiser can afford to make a TV ad – and that’s where Waymark comes in.

Waymark’s software turns a brand’s inputs into a finished video ad in a matter of minutes, complete with a custom script, visuals and voiceover. Local media sellers, including Spectrum Reach, Comcast, NBCU and Fox already use it to produce linear and CTV spots for local advertisers.

In Viant’s view, Waymark addresses three problems: the high cost of producing TV-quality ads, creative fatigue and ads that aren’t tailored to the audience.

Production costs keep most small and midsize advertisers out of CTV, said Viant’s COO, Chris Vanderhook, and so “the down market opportunity is incredible.”

But big enterprise advertisers also need more creative. They run the same ads over and over again until people just tune them out, Tim Vanderhook said.

“It’s not that the creative is bad,” he said, “it’s that they do a big production shoot, they have that creative in market for three to six months and users are overfrequented.”

Viant’s TVision panel data suggests that when someone has seen an ad too many times, their attention plummets, but fresh creative can increase their attention by more than 80%.

The final part of the equation is targeting. Viant plans to pair Waymark with its Household ID, Iris Content ID and TVision’s attention data to tailor different creative versions to specific audiences and also to what they’re watching.

Take an online university that’s trying to reach prospective students. Instead of running a single ad for everyone, the advertiser could have one about athletics, another about academics, a third about campus life and so on.

Viant would use its Household ID to match an ad to the right audience (sports fans, say, or academically minded prospects). The content ID would contextually target the ad to whatever’s on the screen (the athletics ad during a sports game and the academic ad during an ad break in a documentary). And then TVision could measure attention.

Chris Vanderhook referred to this process as “the transformation of creative from a fixed asset into a dynamic asset.”

Even so, for now at least, Waymark is more of a bet than a business. Viant expects it to add little revenue this quarter or next year. But the deal does fit the pattern. Viant is going for those CTV dollars.

“The paradigm is shifting,” Tim Vanderhook said. “TV is no longer reserved only for the world’s largest brands.”

TIME is using AI agents to draft proposals and troubleshoot campaigns – but not to replace the human relationships that drive ad sales.

Why the midterms may not spell doom for ad tech consolidation. Plus, how sports leagues are putting ad revenue before player safety.

Agentic media buying is the No. 1 topic du jour in ad tech discussion circles. But how does agentic buying even work when it comes to buying TV and streaming ads? And how does that workflow differ from programmatic? The startup Swivel aims to address those questions.

AppLovin is growing at a blistering pace, but Wall Street investors remain cautious about the business.

High-end ad blockers mimic some of the same behavior as bot traffic. So WiseGuyGaming repurposed the tools it was already using to identify bots to reveal its ad-blocking audience as well.

Criteo has weathered considerable storms in its day, including a painful moment in March 2020 when its market cap bottomed out below $500 million. Can it pull off yet another turnaround?

#7493. Just a quarter of U.S. adults trust creators to always disclose brand deals

Just one in four U.S. adults believe content creators consistently disclose brand ties when promoting a sponsored product.

That’s not a lot of trust for an industry that relies on creators building close bonds with their audiences.

The data comes from a Morning Consult survey conducted for Business Insider; around 2,000 people participated.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, older folks were less inclined to trust creators: 53% of Baby Boomers said creators “rarely or never” clearly disclose paid deals, while just 21% of Gen Z said the same thing.

Morning Consult also asked respondents whether creators should have to disclose paid sponsorships at all. Across all age groups, the majority of people said yes.

But some did say no: 12% of Boomers, 18% of Gen Xers, 22% of Millennials, and 23% of Gen Z’ers.

We find this wild, and if you’ll forgive a second of conjecture, we’re wondering if the striking number of nos among Millennials and Gen Z has to do with people in those generations being raised in a culture of online side hustles and low barriers to content creation. How many of these respondents are creators themselves, or wish they were, or think they could be, if they just started making TikTok Shop promo videos like their friends and coworkers?

To them, it might seem like a drag to make a video hoping to earn a quick buck, only to have to admit “Yeah, I’m selling something,” in an obvious place.

It seems that way to some established creators and brands, too. BI also cited a recent survey from SheSpeaks where 14% of creators admitted they don’t always disclose brand ties, and 18% said that within the past year, a brand had explicitly asked them not to disclose that they had been paid.

If you’re a regular Tubefilter reader, you will of course know that behavior is very against Federal Trade Commission regulations, and could open violative creators and businesses up to hefty fines. There is never an excuse for an individual creator failing to disclose, but a business that makes it standard to push creators not to disclose is even more problematic.

And while disclosures might seem like a drag to these creators and businesses, to most other people, transparency is reassuring.

Emily Steele, CEO of creator marketing platform Hummingbirds, told BI another key aspect here is that creators need to have meaningful and engaging content outside of brand deals for their audiences to be open when they endorse a product.

“There are creators who only post UGC or sponsored content without any cohesion around what they’re posting about and why,” she said. “Why would I, as a follower, trust you when I feel like all you post is a paid brand deal?”

#7473. Top 50 Most Subscribed YouTube Channels Worldwide • Week Of 11/08/2026

[Editor’s Note: Tubefilter Charts is a weekly rankings column from Tubefilter with data provided by GospelStats. It’s exactly what it sounds like; a top number ranking of YouTube channels based on statistics collected within a given time frame. Check out all of our Tubefilter Charts with new installments every week right here.]

Scroll down for this week’s Tubefilter Chart. 👇

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Though a creator based in Turkey is dominating the Global Sub Top 50, India is still the most ubiquitous country in the ranking. 14 of the top 50 channels hail from that nation, and a few of them have discovered a science experiment that reliably delivers millions of views each day.

Want to feel old? This video arrived on YouTube more than two decades ago.

Once upon a time, the combination of Diet Coke and Mentos produced a viral online video trend. Millions of viewers tuned in as amateur scientists performed backyard experiments, turning ordinary soda bottles into towering fountains of bubbling spray.

The Diet Coke and Mentos trend has survived into the era of YouTube Shorts, but it’s not nearly the fad it once was. Instead, creators have found another combination that produces a terrific reaction: ENO antacids and water.

ENO tablets are similar to Alka-Seltzer, in that they are effervescent antacids capable of curing tummy troubles. The products differ in their active ingredients and the regions where they are most commonly consumed. ENO is a common drugstore find across South Asia.

Some Indian creators have figured out a trick that turns a humble ENO tablet into an improvised firecracker. By injecting water directly into ENO packages, those creators produce localized reactions that cause the packets to explode after a few seconds.

Here’s what makes the ENO videos extra intriguing: The channels uploading these clips are including shoppable links that viewers can use to pick up the tablets for themselves. It’s as if the Diet Coke and Mentos channels from back in the day had sold those products right there on the screen (which, let’s be honest, if YouTube had its shopping tools back then, there definitely would have been some in-app Mentos purchases going on).

The ENO trend’s commercial ties give it legs. Creators aren’t just encouraged to try out this experiment because it gets them views. They can also profit from it directly, and the homemade firecrackers only take a few seconds to set up.

And if you don’t live in a region where ENO tablets are available, well, maybe it’s time to bring back Diet Coke and Mentos. Everything old on the internet eventually becomes new again, and as one of YouTube’s oldest trends comes back around, the creators peddling it can even work in some sales, too.

Fingerprint's device intelligence platform processes billions of identification events for companies that need to know who — or what — is on the other end of a request. Increasingly, the answer is not a person. AI agents, AI assistants, crawlers, headless browsers, and malicious automation now make up a large and fast-growing share of internet traffic, and telling them apart from humans — and from each other — is becoming one of the most important problems our customers ask us to solve.

We are standing up a dedicated Automation Intelligence engineering team to own that problem end to end: detection in the browser, detection at the edge, the classification taxonomy that tells customers what kind of automation they're seeing and how confident we are, and the API that customers and their agents call.

We're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead this team. You'll inherit a small, senior group (three engineers to start, growing to four or five) and a clear mandate. You report directly to the VP of Engineering.

This is a hands-on-adjacent engineering manager role for a small, senior, high-leverage team. You are not expected to write the production code — your engineers and their agents do that — but you are expected to be close enough to it to set direction, evaluate the work, and hold the quality bar.

The team has unusual autonomy and unusual visibility. It owns a product that leadership considers strategically critical, it is the first team operating Fingerprint's AI-native engineering model, and its results — good and bad — will be used as evidence for how the rest of engineering works. That means two things: you'll have real room to decide how the team operates, and you'll need to be honest about what the data shows.

In the first 90 days you will likely: finalize the roster and ownership lines with the sibling team, get the quality loop and engineering baselines running, deliver the engineering evidence for the Beta gate, and run the first review of the AI-native operating model.

#7467. As brands dive into ChatGPT, OpenAI will let them track their mentions

If AI chatbots are going to remain a relevant touchpoint for marketers, then agencies and brands need access to the same analytics they use in their other campaigns. Rumor has it that OpenAI is developing new tools in that area, potentially creating new opportunities for advertisers on ChatGPT.

The rumor in question comes from Juozas Kaziukėnas, the founder of research firm Marketplace Pulse. On LinkedIn, Kaziukėnas posted a screenshot that shows a prompt to “claim your business in ChatGPT.” Among other perks, those who stake their claims will be able to track how often ChatGPT mentions their business within its replies.

Kaziukėnas said that he first noticed the claiming option in August, but he now believes it is close to launching. Multiple sources told Digiday that the business tracker will plot mentions and clicks on a dashboard that will depict day-to-day metrics.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

From a marketing standpoint, that’s a rudimentary level of analytics, but by showing brands their ChatGPT mentions, OpenAI can give them tangible evidence of the results of any marketing pushes they make on the platform. As answer engine optimization becomes a valuable marketing category — and the firms running AEO campaigns haul in big funding rounds — OpenAI is bringing improved measurement to that ecosystem.

If ChatGPT’s brand dashboard is indeed a play for AEO dollars, it will help answer a question that has followed the chatbot ever since its 2023 ascension: What is the best way for OpenAI to monetize its prized technology? Despite early experiments like the GPT Store, ChatGPT’s share of the LLM market has been shrinking. To bring in more revenue, OpenAI started running ads for lower-tier ChatGPT users, even though CEO Sam Altman previously expressed his distaste for that format.

Fast forward a few months, and AEO is now gaining favor. A recent report from AI search analytics platform Peec AI showed that YouTube videos show up far more frequently in chatbot responses and Google’s AI Search Overview when the descriptions of those videos receive edits. The message is clear: Tech companies want brands to play around with major chatbots, and OpenAI is equipping those brands with the metrics they need to analyze their experiments.

#7465. Twitch and Amazon want to turn “git gud” into “u good?” for men’s mental health

Online multiplayer gamers face genuine psychological warfare. Don’t believe me? Log on to your local Apex Legends, Call of Duty, or League of Legends lobby and let the “git guds” (and, well, lots of other stuff we’d rather not print) roll in.

But Twitch, its parent Amazon, and a new organization called GamerCounsel are hoping to change “git gud” into “u gud?”

Timed for Movember, an annual monthlong recognition of the need for more thorough and compassionate healthcare for men, the Squad Support campaign taps Australian Twitch streamers Bajo, Crayator, Jack Buzza, and Midbeast to promote checking in our your gamer buds and–when needed–chatting with licensed professionals about what’s on your mind.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The licensed experts Squad Support recommends are, of course, those from GamerCounsel. The service launched in 2026, and says it brings “professional counselling and psychotherapy into gaming and interactive online spaces.”

Just like an IRL mental health office, GamerCounsel intakes clients and matches them with qualified therapists. The twist here is that therapists aren’t sitting behind desks and clients aren’t lying on couches.

Instead, they’re both squadding up in the same video game.

GamerCounsel therapists and clients (in both one-on-one and group settings) meet remotely over platforms like Discord and work through an appointment while button-mashing together. The org’s website recommends games like Minecraft, Roblox, Fortnite, Rocket League, Stardew Valley, Among Us, Animal Crossing, Mario Kart, Fall Guys, and Destiny, but says its services extend to the thousands of other games on Steam, too–so clients don’t seem super limited in what they can pick.

According to ContentGrip, GamerCounsel is allotting 500 hours of support time to people who see the Squad Support campaign and want to access its gaming-themed help.

A graphic for the campaign illustrates the constant mixed messages male gamers might want to work through with a therapist: “Git gud. But ask for help. Be a man. But don’t be masculine. Share your feelings. But don’t give the ick. Make the first move. But don’t be a creep. Be romantic. But don’t simp. Be the provider. But be present. Be strong. Be vulnerable. Toughen up. Open up. Green flag. Red flag. Red pill. Blue pill. Say less. Say more.”

The Squad Support campaign is going out through Amazon Ads, and includes Twitch components like a new “U GUD?” emote, interactive polls, fundraising tools, and use of Twitch’s Stream Together feature, which Bajo, Crayator, Jack Buzza, Midbeast, and other creators can use to host Movember experts on their streams.

“Gen Z and young millennials are connecting through gaming, and Squad Support meets them where they are. Our first collaboration with Movember brings together a shared ambition to reach young people through the communities and experiences they already value,” Willie Pang, Managing Director of Amazon Ads Australia and New Zealand, said in a statement. “By combining Twitch creators, engaged communities and interactive experiences, Amazon Ads, through Twitch’s Brand Partnership Studio, is demonstrating how brands can go beyond traditional advertising to show up in culture and build meaningful connections with audiences that are notoriously difficult to reach and engage.”

Folks who want to access Squad Support’s free help from GamerCounsel must be 18+ and located in Australia. The org asks that people submit applications, and it will accommodate as many as possible into solo and group therapy sessions.

Here at Tubefilter, we’ve talked many times about creators’ need for mental health support. But this need extends beyond individual communities. Everyone needs more mental health support–especially people who spend their lives being told they shouldn’t.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Guide: AI Max Drove 68% Of Retail Invalid Clicks

Improve lead quality by feeding qualification and revenue data back to ad platforms, so automated bidding can prioritize business outcomes over form fills.

This month, a really good question came in:

“My campaigns are generating plenty of leads and hitting our CPA target, but the sales team says the quality is getting worse. How can I optimize for better leads rather than just more conversions?”

The short answer is: If you want better leads, you first need to teach the platform what a better lead looks like.

It’s very easy to lose track of real-world performance when platform-reported performance looks great. Your CPA may be within target and lead volume may look healthy, while your sales team is telling you those leads aren’t turning into meaningful opportunities.

Those two things aren’t necessarily contradictory.

The ad platform may actually be doing exactly what you asked it to do: finding more of the conversions you told it were valuable. If every form fill is treated as the same conversion equally valuable, the bidding system doesn’t inherently know that one became a strong sales opportunity and another went nowhere.

That means improving lead quality starts with the definition of success you’re giving the platform.

In this post, we’ll look at how to define a better outcome, pass that information back to the platform, and give automated bidding enough meaningful signal and time to optimize toward it.

A quick disclosure: I am a Microsoft Advertising employee, and while I’ll reference Microsoft Advertising capabilities where they’re useful, these principles can apply to paid media programs across platforms.

Before changing your bidding strategy or implementing a new measurement tool, ask a more fundamental question:

What actually makes one lead better than another for your business?

For some advertisers, the initial form fill may be meaningful enough. For others, a more granular segmentation might be needed:

The goal should be to get as close as you reasonably can to the deepest meaningful funnel outcome you can reliably measure.

If 100 leads came through but only 10 were SQLs, you don’t want to teach the bidding system that all 100 were equally valuable simply because they completed the same form.

The closer your conversion tracking gets to the outcome the business actually cares about, the more meaningful the information you’re giving the bidding system.

That’s also why marketing and sales alignment matters here. If the platform says CPA is great while Sales says lead quality is deteriorating, both things can be true.

Before optimizing for “better leads,” make sure everyone agrees on what better actually means. Check that your Sales team is using current lead quality to inform their decisions rather than applying historical bias, as lead quality can change and improve over time with campaign optimizations.

See also: The Conversion Setup Errors That Break Smart Bidding

Once you’ve defined the outcome, the next step is giving the platform information that helps distinguish higher-value actions from lower-value ones.

This is where real-world qualification and revenue data become particularly useful. The best signal any ad platform can work off of is conversion values, and passing accurate values will ensure budgets are directed effectively. This is why conversion value rules are so effective: by adapting the conversion value based on probability of value, you can make it even easier for ad platforms to deliver the right leads.

If you aren’t going to use real-world numbers or outcomes, your CPA or ROAS goals may need to be treated as directional guidance rather than representations of actual business results.

There will also be cases where your ultimate outcome doesn’t happen frequently enough to give conversion-based bidding sufficient volume and signal to effectively optimize performance.

That’s where an earlier but still meaningful conversion can help. A lead becoming marketing-qualified, sales-qualified, or progressing further into your funnel tells you more about lead quality than an unrelated engagement metric.

A useful benchmark for automated bidding is at least 30 conversions within 30 days. Following significant changes to budgets or targets, conversion-based bidding can take as many as roughly 50 conversions to calibrate according to multiple platforms.

See also: Ask A PPC: What Are Learning Periods In Digital Marketing?

Once you know which outcomes matter, you need a way to pass that information back to the platform.

If you can’t yet measure true value, identify the most meaningful signal you can track reliably and use conversion value rules to assign it directional value. If you’re able to measure and optimize against real value, use offline conversion imports to bring that data into your ads platform. This can fill in the gaps so platforms optimize against real value.

That’s where mechanisms such as offline conversions and Conversions APIs come in.

Offline conversions let you connect outcomes that happen after the immediate website experience back to the original ad interaction. Think about someone who clicks an ad, fills out a form, talks to a sales contact, and eventually becomes a customer.

Microsoft Advertising, for example, documents the Click ID, conversion time, and conversion goal name among the core information used for offline conversion imports.

And Conversions API, commonly called CAPI, lets conversion information move programmatically from your systems into the ad platform rather than relying exclusively on periodic manual uploads.

Microsoft Advertising’s Conversions API lets advertisers send conversion and engagement events directly from their servers using Universal Event Tracking (UET), and can pass business signals including revenue, product details, click IDs, hashed identifiers, and consent status.

The mechanism isn’t the strategy. The quality of the signal you’re sending through it is.

Before automating the flow of conversion data, make sure you trust the data you’re automating.

If your CRM is treating poor-quality leads as successful outcomes, passing that information back faster won’t solve the problem. You’ll simply create a more efficient feedback loop around the wrong definition of success.

This also applies to gaps in volume or value of conversions. Advertisers should confirm where the gap is appearing:

Auditing for these factors, as much as the technical passing through of conversion data, is a critical step in closing the loop.

See also: Is Your Conversion Data Misleading You? Seven Common Google Ads Tracking Issues

There is one more piece that can easily get overlooked: conversion delay.

Your campaign may look one way when you initially review results and very different after enough time has passed for leads to move through the sales process.

Microsoft Advertising conversion tracking supports configurable conversion windows, depending on the goal, from one minute up to 90 days.

CAPI introduces another consideration. On Microsoft Advertising, CAPI currently has a 90-day look-back window. Consider which outcomes realistically happen soon enough to pass back through that mechanism.

Your systems still need time for sales to work the lead or for a customer to actually convert.

Your reporting cadence should reflect your actual sales cycle, and automated bidding needs enough meaningful data and time to learn.

That may mean resisting the instinct to make aggressive changes because yesterday’s platform numbers don’t yet contain outcomes that take weeks to materialize.

Everything above assumes the campaign’s purpose is ultimately a conversion-driven business outcome.

If you’re running an awareness or consideration campaign, it may generate sales and booked demos, but these should be reported as secondary key performance indicators rather than the appropriate immediate measures of success. Instead of forcing every campaign into the same CPA or ROAS framework, start by being explicit about the business outcome the campaign is intended to drive and select measurement signals appropriate to that objective.

The important thing is consistency between what you want the campaign to accomplish and what you’re asking the platform to optimize toward.

Conversion totals also don’t explain everything happening between an ad interaction and the eventual outcome.

That’s where diagnostic signals can be useful.

Search behavior can help you understand whether you’re creating interest. Search term reporting, for example, can surface changes in branded searches or the kinds of queries coming from your audience.

Microsoft Clarity can help diagnose what happens after the click. Behavioral analytics such as recordings, heatmaps, and engagement insights from your website can help surface whether visitors are meaningfully exploring the site, encountering friction, or leaving without taking the intended action. Clarity AI Visibility can add another discovery signal by showing when content is cited in supported AI-generated experiences and which AI grounding queries triggered those citations.

These signals aren’t substitutes for your business outcome.

Instead, use them to help answer questions the conversion number alone can’t: Are we creating interest? Where are we losing it? Is campaign performance the problem, or is something happening later in the customer journey?

If you want better leads, don’t just ask your ad platform for more conversions. Teach it what a better conversion looks like.

Start by defining the deepest meaningful outcome you can reliably measure. Then pass qualification, revenue, or other value signals back where appropriate, so the platform has a better understanding of what success means to your business.

Use offline conversions, CAPI, or other feedback mechanisms to connect those real-world outcomes with advertising activity. And make sure you’re giving automated bidding enough meaningful signal and enough time to learn from it.

If you choose not to pass those real-world outcomes back, that’s valid too. Just be honest about what your platform metrics represent and keep your internal source of truth at the center of your business decisions.

The platform can only optimize toward the definition of success you give it.

So when lead volume looks great, but quality doesn’t, don’t immediately ask the bidding system to find more.

First, make sure you’ve taught it what “better” means.

New holiday data counts ads inside Google AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT across five shopping categories and shows which prompts ChatGPT ads ran on.

Adthena reported that approximately 175,100 paid ad placements were found within Google’s AI Overview panel as well as AI Mode panels inside the U.S. during the period of June to September. This included five holiday shopping categories; however, the majority of these paid placements belonged to apparel and consumer electronics.

The Holiday AI Paid Search Report also counts 204,489 ChatGPT ad placements in the same five categories over the same months. Adthena sells ad tracking for Google and ChatGPT, and the report closes with an offer for a free trial of its ChatGPT Ads product.

Some U.S. apparel and electronics advertisers may already be using portions of their existing campaigns to serve ads to users who see AI Overviews and AI Mode. The report identifies where the ads appeared, but does not track which ads were clicked, how much was spent, nor what conversions were achieved on either surface.

The total number of ads in Google’s AI Answers (in the U.S.) in this report is based upon a combined total for both AI Overviews and AI Mode. In that count, apparel has approximately 111,000 placements; consumer electronics have about 55,000; travel has roughly 6,500; beauty has about 2,100; and toys and games have around 685.

There are no separate ad buys for these placement types. According to Google’s Help Page regarding Ads in AI-Powered Experiences, all Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns that exist are automatically eligible to appear in AI-Answers. Although advertisers cannot specifically target only AI Overviews or AI Mode, or opt out of those placements apart from Search, they may still utilize negative keyword targeting and/or brand exclusions.

The report also reviewed how many times AI Overviews appeared in Google Results for both August of 2025 and August of 2026. Going from 304 million to 575 million, U.S. appearances saw an 89% increase over that period. The UK/EU saw an increase of 160%, while Australia saw an increase of 536%. The report doesn’t describe the queries behind those counts or say whether the set stayed the same across both years.

The report counts 204,489 ChatGPT Ads placements across five categories, Apparel, Consumer Electronics, Travel, Toys & Games and Beauty, from June through September 2026.

Adthena’s press release frames it more broadly, stating more than 200,000 advertisement placements occurred since OpenAI started allowing others to buy advertising space on the chatbot.

In the report’s count, apparel accounted for the largest number of advertisement placements at 90,517. Next was Consumer Electronics with 56,569; then Travel with 48,134; followed by Toys and Games with 4,694 and lastly Beauty with 4,575.

In addition, the company reported that there were 1,082 different advertisers in those five categories using the service in June, 3,741 advertisers in July, and 6,333 advertisers in August. The company projected the number of advertisers in September.

According to the report, the advertisers in its data in Toys and Games increased the most during that time frame from June to August, increasing 13 fold, from what the company calls a relatively low base.

The report states that the total number of advertiser placements included in their research covered all markets, but does not identify which markets or state whether they continued to monitor the same market(s)/queries throughout the entire four-month period. In addition, OpenAI expanded its footprint during that time.

On August 18, OpenAI announced that ChatGPT Ads would be available in 31 European countries. The company began offering this service one week later. Additionally, on September 23, OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Ads to seven additional Asian markets.

For perspective, on October 21 OpenAI stated that more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT Ads since the advertising capability was opened up to outside parties just over eight months earlier. This figure represents all categories and the complete period of time that ChatGPT Ads has been open to third-party advertisers, so it isn’t directly comparable to the report’s monthly counts.

In addition to that, the report groups ChatGPT ads based on the nature of the search that an ad was run against. It describes research and discovery queries as “people comparing or asking what’s best rather than naming a product.”

In beauty, 83% of ads ran on those queries, while travel and toys & games were at 69% and 67% respectively. Apparel and consumer electronics came in under half, at 48% and 42% respectively.

Again, the press release references only the data related to beauty, travel and toys. The report provides no information about how questions were categorized.

Since Google includes searches that prompt ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode in aggregate in its standard reports for all of Search, they are intermingled throughout your search terms report.

In ChatGPT, best-of and comparison prompts carried most of the observed ads in beauty, travel & toys, and less than 50% of those seen in apparel and electronics.

After the report’s time frame closed, Google’s ads within their AI answers continued to evolve. Google announced that they were launching multi-turn ads in the United States on October 28. These allow advertisers’ ads to show up on subsequent searches (queries) in AI Mode. In addition, Google stated that ads in AI Mode are scaling to ten additional countries including Canada and Australia. They further stated that Brazil, Mexico and the United Kingdom were planned for Q4 2026.

OpenAI’s October 21 announcement expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries. The most recent Adthena data is from September so does not include these new developments nor the weeks surrounding Black Friday.

#7457. Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models.

In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts.

On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then.

“I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'”

Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.”

Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place.

As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold):

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements. The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.”

A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “Ad Creative Generative AI Terms” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand.

Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements.

“[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.”

University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house.

“You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said.

Prior to the update on Friday, the European Publishers Council announced that it would formally petition the E.U.’s telecommunications regulatory authorities and its executive body, the European Commission, to “scrutinize these terms urgently, including their implications for copyright, contractual fairness and abuse of market power.”

The United Kingdom News Media Association, the trade organization representing British media, issued a statement on Friday calling for government officials to intervene.

“This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber. “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.”

The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “outrageous and probably illegal.”

“The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power,” Coffey said. “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.”

This story has been updated to include comments from Meta.

#7455. “Convenings” for CEOs will help Semafor reach a second profitable year

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Semafor expects to have its second profitable year, thanks to a growing events, er, convening business, cofounders Justin Smith and Ben Smith announced.

The news company, which launched four years ago, had its first profitable year last year on $40 million in revenue. In a note published Sunday, Smith and Smith said they expect to close the year “substantially bigger” in “revenue and profitability and reach.”

RELATED ARTICLEThe media startup Semafor launches with a “more honest” article format and lots of global ambitionSarah ScireOctober 18, 2022About half of the company’s revenue comes from live events, which Semafor refers to as “convenings.” A two-day convening in November, for example, will cover “Silicon Valley & The World.” The co-chairs include names like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

In their note, the cofounders wrote that “Semafor is starting to emerge clearly as the thing that we hoped it would become.”

RELATED ARTICLESemafor aims to be the source for “intelligent news consumers” who are “unhappy” and “screaming from the rooftops”Sarah ScireSeptember 7, 2022“We launched with the insight that a leadership audience — CEOs and political leaders alike — was, paradoxically, the most desperate for efficient, fair, and sophisticated news,” they continued.

It’s a stretch to say CEOs and political leaders are “desperate” for news. Existing news consumers tend to be older, wealthier, more white collar, and more politically engaged than those who don’t consume news. The genuinely underserved news audiences are elsewhere. Journalism for “decision makers” is one of the most crowded markets in news. Outlets like Bloomberg, Politico Pro, Financial Times, Punchbowl News, Axios Pro, and The Information operate in a similar space.

But readers aren’t the primary financial supporters of Semafor’s business. That’d be the corporate sponsors paying for access to its audience through ads and events. Although the annual update says the company has 1.2 million subscriptions, those remain free subscriptions for now.

By building a profitable and growing news business, Semafor has done something exceedingly rare. (It now has journalists on the ground in 11 countries and plans to launch in Asia in 2027.) Editor-in-chief Ben Smith explained some of his thinking on an episode of Decoder this summer.

In my memory, we always thought at some point we’d do subscriptions, but in my experience you just cannot be ideological about revenue. It’s hard enough to build a business in news without getting all hung up on the values of the different revenue streams.

Advertising-based publishers will tell you that democracy can only survive in a world where there aren’t paywalls. Subscription publishers will tell you that advertising is corrupting. At some point you realize everyone’s just talking about their book and that sometimes they’re already in a tough business and they’re talking themselves out of incremental opportunities and really successful media companies.

It’s “impossible” for publishers to compete with Google and Meta in the scaled advertising business, Smith told Decoder. He described Semafor as “an anti-scale business.”

If you’re reaching people in a very focused way in various particular environments — in person, in email, in video — that’s a case you can really credibly make to advertisers. We’ve built a big advertising and related convening business that way, and that’s one answer. It’s not the only answer, but it is one.

#7454. November Click Spikes In Google Search Console Are Bot Traffic – How To Filter Your Reports via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

That sudden click spike in Search Console isn’t real traffic. Here’s what my data shows, what’s causing it, and how to filter it out.

Earlier this week, I saw Barry Schwartz’s post on X (and his write-up on Search Engine Roundtable) sharing a screenshot from Joy Hawkins. Joy noticed that several sites were seeing sudden, massive vertical spikes in Google Search Console clicks while impressions stayed flat, and Barry asked a great follow-up question: “Anyone else seeing this? If so, how are you filtering the report…”

Screenshot of Barry Schwartz and Joy Hawkins’ post on X highlighting the sudden click spike in Google Search Console. (Image Credit: Marie Haynes)

When I saw Barry’s tweet, I immediately thought this would be the ultimate real-world test for Marie’s Brain – my soon-to-be-launched agentic SEO and AI search analysis system.

Over the past several months, I have been building Marie’s Brain to combine my 15+ years of research on Google’s ranking systems with live, programmatic access to the Search Console and analytics data of the sites I monitor. Instead of manually clicking through Search Console property by property to see if any of my clients were affected, I asked my system to scan across all of the sites I monitor, check the unfinalized fresh data through Nov. 2, 2026, and flag any property showing a sudden anomaly in clicks.

Within seconds, Marie’s Brain surfaced the exact same vertical spike across multiple sites in completely different industries – and pulled the raw page, query, device, and country dimensions so I could see what was actually happening under the hood.

Just like Glenn Gabe and Joy Hawkins mentioned in Barry’s Search Engine Roundtable post, the majority of properties I monitor showed completely normal traffic. However, while some SEOs saw the wave begin over the weekend (Oct. 31 to Nov. 1), a distinct subset of sites I monitor experienced a dramatic vertical spike on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026 that mirrors Joy’s screenshot:

Six-month daily Google Search Console clicks (Search type: Web, including fresh unfinalized data through Nov. 2, 2026) across three affected properties I monitor. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Here is how those three anonymized properties behaved on Nov. 2, 2026 compared to their prior seven-day baseline (Oct. 26 – Nov. 1, 2026):

When I had my system drill into the raw API rows for Nov. 2, two unmistakable patterns emerged across the affected sites:

Visual summary of why total impressions look flat while automated deep-SERP clicks create a vertical spike in Google Search Console. Image Credit: Marie Haynes

Normally, organic clicks in Search Console are heavily concentrated in the top 3 to 5 results on Page 1. On Nov. 2, click-through rate (CTR) exploded on pages ranking between Position 11 and Position 55 (Pages 2 through 6 of Google):

Why did total impressions stay flat if every click also had an impression? It comes down to simple scale. When a site normally gets 18,000 impressions and 50 clicks per day (like Site A), adding 275 automated impressions is only a 1.5% bump on the impression line – completely invisible on a chart! Adding 275 clicks to a 50-click baseline, on the other hand, creates a massive 6.5x vertical spike.

On Site C (a technical troubleshooting Q&A site), a single long-tail troubleshooting page that normally gets zero to one click per day (and never received more than seven clicks in a single day across the entire previous six months) suddenly jumped to 13 clicks on Nov. 1 and 40 clicks on Nov. 2.

While the spikes on Sites A and B came from U.S. searches, all 40 clicks on this Site C page came from Canada. From Oct. 28 to Oct.r 31, that page only had four to seven impressions per day in Canada (and 0 clicks) while ranking on Page 2. Then on Nov. 2, Canadian impressions on that page jumped by ~45 (to 50 impressions), and Canadian clicks jumped from 0 to 40 clicks – meaning almost every single one of those new impressions was clicked (an 80.0% CTR at average position 14.6 on Page 2, while U.S. clicks on that page stayed at 0)!

When I inspected the exact queries that clicked into that single URL on Nov. 2, there were 23 slightly reworded variations of the exact same troubleshooting question (including systematic number permutations like 3 times, 4 times, 5 times, 7 times, 10 times), almost every single one logging 100% CTR (1 click / 1 impression, 2/2, or 3/3) between Position 10.0 and Position 33.0. Other troubleshooting pages on the same site logged 1 click / 1 impression (100% CTR) at Position 45.5 to 54.0.

Normally, when a basic rank tracker or scraper loads a Google search results page, it only generates impressions – not clicks. For Search Console to record a click, a browser or bot has to actually follow (or trigger) Google’s click-tracking link on the search results page.

Looking at the data patterns across these sites, four possibilities stand out:

Because GSC does not let you filter the top performance chart by ranking position or CTR, there is no perfect one-click button to strip only the bot clicks out of your sitewide graph if dozens of pages were affected. However, these three approaches work well depending on how your site was impacted:

If dozens of pages across your whole site spiked on Desktop (like Sites A & B), you cannot exclude every page individually. While filtering the top bar by Device: Mobile obviously hides your legitimate Desktop traffic too, it is a great sanity check to show a client or stakeholder that your Mobile organic trendline is completely normal (on Site A, Mobile clicks were 30 on Nov 2 vs. 27-40 on prior days; on Site B, Mobile clicks were 11 on Nov 2 vs. 11 on Nov 1).

To see the exact pages that were affected on your site:

If you have Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, or an agentic coding environment (like Antigravity or Cursor) connected to the Google Search Console API or a custom MCP server, you can paste this exact prompt to check all of your sites in seconds:

No. Because this is automated activity rather than human visitors, you do not need to change your pages, disavow anything, or panic when those clicks drop right back down to baseline. Just annotate early November 2026 in your reporting (right alongside GSC’s other recent reporting changes) so you and your clients know why Search Console suddenly showed a vertical jump in clicks!

#7453. When hackers become sources: Inside the new craft of reporting on hacked data

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“You’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.”

Some consequential reporting of recent years has emerged thanks to what is normally defined as a “hack-and-leak,” a specific kind of cyberattack that results in the release of the information obtained by hackers. When Anonymous and allied collectives breached corporations and state agencies during the hacktivist wave of the 2010s, for instance, they turned stolen data into front-page news.

Reporters covering the invasion of Ukraine have frequently worked with documents pulled from Russian institutions by hackers of different allegiances. Hacktivists have breached surveillance vendors and spyware firms, granting journalists direct and exclusive access to the internal files of companies that sell to repressive governments. Ransomware gangs, cybercriminal groups, and state-affiliated hackers deposit fresh troves of hacked data on the open internet, or route it to the public through intermediaries like Distributed Denial of Secrets.

How are journalists responding to these reporting scenarios? For my research, recently published in Journalism Practice, I interviewed 10 journalists across the U.S. and Europe who work or have worked with hacked data. Some of them specialize in the coverage of cyber issues; others mainly focus on current affairs and global conflict. These journalists work for a variety of news outlets, from investigative reporting newsrooms to general interest outlets and technology brands, and have engaged with hacker sources at various levels.

The journalists I spoke with paint a picture of an emerging craft, rather than a settled method. Here’s some of what I found.

There are no fixed guidelines or established and shared practices on how to handle and report on hacked material in news reporting. Instead, the methods are being developed by practitioners on a case by case basis. One reporter who works for an investigative newsroom told me:

Hackers themselves are becoming increasingly strategic about their relationships with the press. One reporter following a specific cyber beat emphasized this:

“I’d say that [hackers] of all kinds love to flex and get credit. A lot of them don’t, but many absolutely do. I’m not sure if the desire to flex has increased, but you’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.

That maturity means developing awareness of how a story will be framed and disseminated and calculating which journalist to approach. Hackers now may select their outlets of choice, matching a leak to the reporter who they think is capable of understanding the story and carrying it further.

There are different kinds of hackers, wearing different and/or multiple hats. Interviewees drew distinctions between financially motivated cybercriminals, whose leaks are often equivalent to extortion by other means, and state-affiliated actors, who may also pose as independent hacktivists to launder politically motivated leaks into credible coverage.

At the same time, some hackers or hacker collectives — like Phineas Fisher, known for his activist remit against surveillance companies — may act for political and public interest–oriented reasons, reaching out to journalists to expose wrongdoing, unethical issues, or crimes. Notoriously, though, hacking is not a field in which hats are worn straightforwardly: Identities, definitions and agendas, including mere trolling, may blur into one another.

Hacked material needs to be handled with a great deal of skepticism. When working with hacked sources, one journalist said, it’s a matter of “treating every dataset as if it has chlamydia.” But the verification techniques the journalists said they use — such as confirming that an email address exists in a company’s records, cross-referencing with known facts, or examining a file for signs of tampering — are fairly conventional. This type of reporting requires more disclosures, especially when a source’s identity can’t be established. One journalist working in this area said:

I think you should be very transparent about that in your reporting. You should say something like, “We don’t know who the source is; it could be the GRU [Russian Federation] or whoever, but we have confirmed that this data is real and this is what it shows.”

Declared openly, the uncertainty may become a meaningful part of the story itself.

Source protection is further complicated when it comes to hackers. Some interviewees extend the full protection they would give any source to hackers, refusing to assist law enforcement even if the source is a self-declared criminal. Others prefer to know as little as possible about their sources, framing the choice as harm reduction for both parties. As one journalist in my sample put it:

The less I know about these things, the harder it’s going to be for me to burn my source or to publish something that inadvertently turns out to be harmful to my source.

Reporters working exclusively with material already circulating online in cybercrime forums or other repositories on the web treat source protection as beside the point, because the origins of the information cannot be traced and because the material is in effect “out there.”

Beneath all of this sits the finding with the widest implications: Ethical decisions in this domain resist strict codification. No general rule can be written in advance, the reporters I spoke with suggested, and judgment in the individual case is the only workable guide. Is publishing hacked material justified? It depends on the specifics of the case at hand, one reporter told me.

I kind of think it all depends on what you’re exposing. Maybe it’s generally wrong to break into people’s computers and steal data, but if you’re exposing serious crimes, then I think it can be justified.

Interviewees described practical wisdom under pressure: the ability to read a specific situation and act appropriately n it, without having the opportunity to refer to an established code or checklist.

Newsrooms, meanwhile, may need to develop verification standards suited to information of illicit origin, transparency norms that treat uncertainty as something to disclose rather than paper over, and a shared language for the ethical judgments that journalists currently make case by case on their own.

Philip Di Salvo is a senior researcher and lecturer at the Institute for Media and Communications Management at the University of St. Gallen, Switzerland. Adobe Stock

#7451. Two out of five Americans regularly get their news on Facebook

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Despite what my Facebook feed looks like, the platform’s not just for AI fruit videos and birthday posts.

According to data from the Pew Research Center published Monday, 40% of adults in the United States regularly get their news from Facebook.

That’s up from 36% in 2020, signaling the continued stability of the platform as a news source — a trend that the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism observed in its Digital News Report this year. As we reported in June, people around the world are increasingly abandoning news websites for social media.

The Center surveyed 5,600 U.S. adults in late August as part of its American Trends Panel, and asked respondents several questions about their news and social media habits. Pew did not give respondents a definition of “news,” instead letting them use their own understanding of the term when they filled out the survey. More than half (59%) said that they get news from social media “often or sometimes,” but only 19% actually prefer social media as a place to get news.

Of Facebook news consumers, 33% are men and 49% are between the ages of 30 and 49. The platform is most popular for women (47%), Hispanic Americans (51%), Americans with a high school diploma or less (46%), and Republicans (43%).

Regular news consumption among American users has increased on nine of the 12 social media platforms that Pew studied, including YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), Reddit, Nextdoor, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. News consumption has either dropped or stayed the same on Rumble, Truth Social, and Bluesky.

The second-most regularly used platform among American adults is YouTube (34%), followed by Instagram (23%), TikTok (20%), and X (10%). YouTube news consumers are more likely to be male (41%), between ages 18 and 29 (39%), and identify as Black (47%) or Asian (53%). Republicans (35%) and Democrats (36%) are equal YouTube news consumers.

The most regularly used platform for news among young adults is Instagram (43%), followed by Facebook (40%), TikTok and YouTube (both 39%), and X and Reddit (both 18%).  The Center found that 20% of U.S. adults now regularly get their news on TikTok, up from 3% in 2020. Of TikTok users, 53% reported getting news regularly on the platform. Nextdoor users are also increasingly turning to the neighborhood forum app for information. In 2026, 45% of Nextdoor users reported regularly getting news from the app, up from 23% in 2022.
